Posted October 21, 2003
Analysis by Richard Cowan
Inasmuch as even Gray Davis must recognize that his political career is finished, he was probably sincere when he signed Senator Vasconcellos SB 420 that is supposed to clarify the medical cannabis situation in California. However, the California medical cannabis movement is split on the issue.
See
American Medical Marijuana Association Opposes SB420. Supports Conservative State Senator For Governor.

As I said last month, my greatest objection is simply that I don't think that much of the California police will act in good faith, no matter what compromises are attempted.
See
Sociopathic Law Enforcement, Cannabis Prohibition, and the Stockholm Syndrome. We Must Call Lies Lies Before We Can Call Ourselves Truly Free.

Certainly the bill has some excellent features. That is why so many activists supported it.

My friend Chris Conrad lists a variety of positive points in SB 420:
 SB 420 was the result of much input from patients and reformers
It recognizes all patient's rights as embodied in Prop 215 as summarized in SB420 Section 1(a)(1)
Participation in the voluntary ID program is not a requirement for full protection under Prop 215 11362.71(f)
It asserts medical marijuana as a matter of states rights 420 (1)(e)
It extends the power of recommendation/approval to osteopaths 11362.7(a)
It allows agencies to provide medical marijuana to qualified patients 11362.7(d)(2)
It allows caregivers to have more than one patient in the same county 11362.7(d)(3)
It allows caregivers to have one out-of-county patient 11362.7(d)(3)
It creates a completely voluntary and protective 1-year photo ID program for participating patients and/or caregivers. 11362.71(a)(1)
It provides " around the clock " validation of participation in the program when police confront a patient or caregiver 11362.71(a)(2)
It allows non-governmental agencies to process the cards 11362.71(c)
It promises confidentiality of records 11362.71(d)(1)
It stops arrests -- not just prosecutions -- of qualified individuals for possession, transportation, delivery or cultivation up to a very minimal level of 8 oz and 6 plants per patient (that could arguably be hash or hash oil, which would be equivalent to more; I'm not sure what it does about tinctures, which have a lot of liquid weight) 11362.71(e)
It includes the right for individual to appeal if rejected for patient ID card 11362.74 (b)
It gives Medi-Cal patients a 50% fee discount 11362.755(a)
It allows transportation and processing (HS 11360) 11362.765 (b)
It reduces the risk of a patient being charged with intent to sell (11359) maintaining a place where cannabis is produced, provided or used (HS11366, 11366.5, 11570 ) 11362.765(b)
It allows reimbursement for a caregiver's material and labor 11362.765(c)
It empowers physicians to grant exemptions for quantities 11362.77 (b)
It allows communities to adopt more realistic amounts but does not allow them to go below the " floor " amounts 11362.77(c)
It codifies the medical use of dried cannabis flowers rather than leaf 11362.77(d)
It opens the door for us to work with the AG to amend these levels upward 11362.77(e)
It recognizes collectives and coop gardens, without regard to county boundaries 11362.775
It requires police to comply with these provisions 11362.78
It recognizes that inmates can use medical marijuana 11362.785(c)
It exempts patients in their homes from the penalties associated with using cannabis within 1000 feet of a school 11362.79(b)
It enables parolees, defendants and probates to retain full access to MMJ 11362.795
It criminalizes breach of confidentiality (eg., giving patient info to the feds) 11362.81(b)(4)

However, all of the good things that the bill might do ultimately depend on the willingness of the narks to obey the law, and that has been the real problem with 215 all along.
See
Selective Enforcement Versus Selective Compliance 2 Articles
and links, especially
California Narks Lie to Justify Disobeying Prop 215. And They Lie About Me In The Process.

The invaluable Fred Gardner interviewed Dennis Peron (among others) and Dennis, the father of 215, said, I am so mad. I can't believe it. The caregiver has to live in the same county? That's wrong -I can't believe Gray Davis signed it. I'm going to sue to get this reversed. They're not allowed to weaken a law that's created by the people's will... I'm pissed at Davis, pissed at Vasconcellos, pissed at Lockyer... And I'm also pissed at the marijuana people. They went like sheep for this.

Dennis may succeed in his challenge, because California initiatives cannot be amended by the state legislature. Prop 215 has no limits on either the number of plants, and as Dennis notes, it does not limit the number of patients a caregiver can have that live in another county.

SB 420 says, " A qualified patient or primary caregiver may possess no more than eight ounces of dried marijuana per qualified patient. In addition, a qualified patient or primary caregiver may also maintain no more than six mature or 12 immature marijuana plants per qualified patient. "

That will not be enough for many patients, but it also says, Counties and cities may retain or enact medical marijuana guidelines allowing qualified patients or primary caregivers to exceed the state limits. "

In that regard, SB 420 would seem to contradict itself by stating in Section 1 (b) (2) that the Legislature seeks to Promote uniform and consistent application of the act among the counties. If it does that, it will be by bringing limits down to the levels set in the bill. That would be disastrous.

Doctors can also set higher limits for their individual patients, but given the harassment of Dr. Tod Mikuriya and other doctors who have been willing to give recommendations, that is problematic at best.
Also see
Dr. Tod Mikuriya Stands Up For Medical Marijuana Users In California Courts

There are also some good things in the bill that really don't necessarily mean very much. It seems to provide for prisoners and people on probation or parole to be able to use medical cannabis, but not quite.

For example, section 11362.785.(a) says, Nothing in this article shall require any accommodation of any medical use of marijuana on the property or premises of any place of employment or during the hours of employment or on the property or premises of any jail, correctional facility, or other type of penal institution in which prisoners reside or persons under arrest are detained.(b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a person shall not be prohibited or prevented from obtaining and submitting the written information and documentation necessary to apply for an identification card on the basis that the person is incarcerated in a jail, correctional facility, or other penal institution in which prisoners reside or persons under arrest are detained. (c) Nothing in this article shall prohibit a jail, correctional facility, or other penal institution in which prisoners reside or persons under arrest are detained, from permitting a prisoner or a person under arrest who has an identification card, to use marijuana for medical purposes under circumstances that will not endanger the health or safety of other prisoners or the security of the facility.

In other words, SB 420 does not require that prisoners be allowed to use medical cannabis, but it does not prohibit it either. The chances of a prisoner being allowed to use medical cannabis in a California prison are slim to none.

Similarly, defendants, probationers and parolees may request that they be allowed to use medical cannabis, but nothing guarantees that they will be allowed to do so.

The bottom line is that SB 420 will help many patients, perhaps even a majority of them, but it will also endanger those who need more than the minimum quantities established by the bill.

Whether or not it protects anyone will ultimately depend on the willingness of the police to obey the law, and SB 420 would not have been necessary at all if the state's Attorney General, Bill Lockyer had been willing to force them to obey Prop 215.
See
California Narks Wage War On Patients and The Law. Impeach Attorney General Lockyer!
and links.

The California Narcotics Officers Association has always opposed medical cannabis, and their paid lobbyist, John Lovell worked to kill it. Inasmuch as they have refused to obey Prop 215, it seems unlikely that they will obey this new and improved version.

In any case, SB 420 is now the law and the medical cannabis community will have to try to make it work and to amend its more dangerous features.

Of course, SB 420 does nothing to stop the depredations of the DEA. It remains to be seen if the new governor is as bold at facing down John Walters as he was against fictional Predators.

One final note, the Supreme Court refused even to hear the Drug Czar's appeal of the 9th Circuit's ruling that keeps the DEA from pulling doctors licenses to prescribe controlled substances, like morphine, for recommending medical cannabis. That means that there were not even four Justices who thought it worth hearing.
See
Federal Judge Stops Drug Czar's Threat To Pull Licenses of Doctors Who Recommend Medical Marijuana.

This may help patients who live in the 9th Circuit find doctors who are less afraid to recommend medical cannabis.
